lines.s10: Chardonnay is the white grape of Burgundy, lemon and green apple when lean, ripe peach and toasted hazelnut when rich.
lines.s20: Chardonnay is Burgundy's white grape, and it takes the shape of the place and the cellar. From a cool site it is lemon, green apple and chalk, and from a warm one or from new oak barrels it is peach, cream and toasted hazelnut.
lines.s45: Chardonnay is the white grape of Burgundy, and it now grows almost everywhere wine is made. On its own it is quiet: lemon, green apple and white peach, dry, with a rounded, medium to full body. The cellar finishes the picture. New oak barrels add toasted hazelnut and vanilla, and a second, softening fermentation adds a note of butter. Burgundy tends to be leaner and more chalky, while California and Australia are often riper and creamier. Pour it with roast chicken, lobster or anything in a butter sauce. Its parents, found by DNA in 1999, are Pinot and a lowly, almost forgotten grape called Gouais Blanc.
lines.sale: Chardonnay is the white that can be whatever the table needs, from chalk and lemon to cream and toasted hazelnut. Tell me the dish and I will pour the lean one for oysters or the rich one for lobster.

glass.lead: Lemon, green apple and white peach on a rounded frame, with toasted hazelnut and cream where the cellar adds new oak.

ladder.where: Chablis and the Côte de Beaune, Champagne, Tasmania
Napa and Sonoma, the Central Coast, Margaret River
California's Central Valley and inland south eastern Australia

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus in a cool site and medium in a warm one, alcohol moderate to high, body medium to full.

old.where: Burgundy, from Chablis to the Mâconnais, and Champagne
old.glass: Tends to be leaner and more restrained: lemon, green apple and white peach over crushed chalk, with bright acidity and moderate alcohol. The place leads and the fruit follows.
old.cellar: Chablis is mostly raised in steel or old casks. The Côte de Beaune ferments in barrel, a share of it new, and rests on its lees.

new.where: California, Oregon, Australia, New Zealand, Chile and South Africa
new.glass: Typically riper and broader: yellow apple, ripe peach and pineapple, with softer acidity, fuller body and higher alcohol. Butter and vanilla often sit in front of the fruit.
new.cellar: Often full malolactic conversion and a larger share of new French oak, with the lees stirred for a creamy texture.

contrast.why: Climate first: more sun and warmth mean riper fruit, lower acidity and higher alcohol. Then the cellar's choices of oak and malolactic conversion. Then the label: Burgundy names a place and its rules, the New World names the grape.
contrast.blur: Cool New World sites such as the Sonoma Coast, Tasmania and the Yarra Valley now make lean, bright wines, and a warm year in Burgundy gives ripe, creamy ones.
contrast.call: Chalk, high acidity and oak held in the background lean Old World; pineapple, butter and vanilla up front lean New World.

service.temp: 50 to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; a lean, unoaked wine a little cooler.
service.glass: A white wine glass for lean styles; a wide Burgundy bowl for rich, oaked wines.
service.decant: Rarely. A young, tightly wound white Burgundy can open with a short decant; taste a sample first.
service.age: Most within two to five years; village and premier cru Burgundy five to ten, the grands crus longer.

with.why: lean, chalky Chablis mirrors the brine
the wine's weight and cream match the roast

with.dish: Lobster or crab with drawn butter
with.why: a rich, oaked Chardonnay echoes the butter
toasted hazelnut in the wine meets the browned butter

labels.means: Chardonnay from northern Burgundy, usually made without new oak: lean, chalky and bright.
Sparkling wine from white grapes alone; in Champagne that is nearly always Chardonnay.
Fermented and aged in steel, so the fruit and the acidity show with no vanilla or toast.
Chardonnay from the Mâconnais in southern Burgundy; not Pouilly-Fumé, which is Loire Sauvignon Blanc.

guest.a: Yes. Chablis is Chardonnay from the cool north of Burgundy, usually made without new oak, so it tastes of lemon, green apple and chalk and not of butter.

guest.q: I do not like oaky, buttery Chardonnay. What should I try?
guest.a: Ask for an unoaked one: Chablis, a Mâcon, or a cool coast wine from Sonoma or Tasmania. The butter and vanilla come from the cellar, not the grape.

guest.q: Why does one Chardonnay taste so different from the next?
guest.a: The grape itself is quiet, so climate and cellar speak loudly. A cool site gives lemon and green apple, a warm one pineapple, and new oak barrels add toast and vanilla.

compare.tell: Chenin Blanc shows higher acidity with quince, honey and a wet wool note; Chardonnay is rounder and takes its accent from oak and lees.
Pinot Gris is oilier, with spiced pear and a faint bitterness; Chardonnay is cleaner in line and shows cream or toast from the cellar.
Viognier is loudly perfumed, all apricot and honeysuckle, with lower acidity; Chardonnay has no such perfume of its own.

cards.front: Chardonnay: where is it at home, and who are its parents?
cards.back: Burgundy, from Chablis to the Mâconnais. DNA work published in 1999 found it to be a cross of Pinot and Gouais Blanc.

cards.front: Old World or New World Chardonnay: what does a blind taster lean on?
cards.back: Chalk, high acidity and oak in the background lean Old World. Pineapple, butter and vanilla up front, with softer acidity and higher alcohol, lean New World.

cards.front: What does the cellar add to Chardonnay, and from what?
cards.back: Butter from malolactic conversion; toasted hazelnut, vanilla and toast from new oak; cream and bread dough from time on the lees.

questions.q: A blind white is pale gold and dry, with pineapple, ripe peach, butter and vanilla, soft acidity and high alcohol. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Tropical ripeness, butter from malolactic conversion and vanilla from new oak on a full body point to a warm New World site. Chablis would be lean, chalky and unoaked.

questions.q: A guest who dislikes buttery, oaky whites still wants a Chardonnay with her oysters. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Chablis is Chardonnay from northern Burgundy, usually made without new oak: lemon, green apple and chalk. Meursault and Napa are typically barrel aged, and Pouilly-Fumé is Sauvignon Blanc.

questions.q: A guest asks what Blanc de Blancs means on a bottle of Champagne. What do you tell him?
opts: White wine from white grapes, nearly always Chardonnay
White wine from black grapes, Pinot Noir or Meunier
A Champagne with no sugar added at the end
A Champagne from a single harvest year
questions.exp: Blanc de Blancs is white wine from white grapes, which in Champagne nearly always means Chardonnay. White from black grapes is Blanc de Noirs.
